Samsung could slip to the second rank in foldables, but that could be a good thing. Reading time: 3 minutes Abhijeet Mishra / SamMobile Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra Apple recently took the wraps off the highly anticipated iPhone Duo. It brings a Galaxy Z Fold 8-like form factor to the masses. While the tech giant is years late to the foldable party Samsung started, Apple's implementation brings some genuinely interesting takes on foldable hardware and software.  Subtle but impactful touches, like a cleverly integrated vertical app dock and incredibly fluid opening and closing UI animations, show a lot of polish.  While the initial reaction might be to panic about Samsung's market share in the foldable category, the reality could be more optimistic. The iPhone Duo may not just make the Galaxy Z Fold 9 better but also turbocharge Samsung’s Galaxy Z series in general.  Abhijeet Mishra / SamMobile                                              Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra                                                                                  While Android foldable phones have been around for years, third-party app optimization has barely improved. Since apps on Apple devices usually receive substantially faster support for newer hardware and software features, the iPhone Duo will undoubtedly get big-screen support with foldable optimizations very soon, which could be excellent news for Galaxy Z users.  Most major developers and firms have apps for both Android and iOS platforms and utilize shared development pipelines. When they bring foldable optimizations to the iPhone Duo, porting those layouts and features to Android foldables becomes easier.  This could very well result in a massive bump in the availability of optimized, foldable, and tablet-ready apps on Galaxy Z phones, solving one of the most persistent software hurdles on Android foldables.  Apple                                              Apple iPhone Duo's inner foldable screen                                                                                  Android foldable phones have been on the market for years, but they are still relatively rare to find in people's hands and are mostly restricted to enthusiasts and early adopters. The entry of the iPhone Duo changes that overnight.  Even though industry projections expect Apple to overtake Galaxy Z series sales by 2027, the iPhone Duo will quickly familiarize the general public with the folding form factor. As millions of people start seeing folding screens in their day-to-day lives, the anxiety around the durability of foldable phones will start disappearing.  Abhijeet Mishra / SamMobile                                              Galaxy Z Fold 8 colors                                                                                  Foldable phones will instantly become more acceptable and aspirational among general consumers who aren't tech enthusiasts. This will encourage more people to buy foldable phones, and many of them will likely prefer Samsung's devices.  Market analysts believe that the iPhone Duo will dramatically increase the sales volume of the foldable phone market. It is true that Samsung’s stronghold on the foldable segment will loosen, and its market share could drop next year. However, reports indicate that the overall sales of Galaxy Z series phones will actually increase in terms of units shipped.  Abhijeet Mishra / SamMobile                                              Galaxy Z Fold 8 vs Fold 8 Ultra                                                                                  Since foldable phones carry a premium price tag compared to traditional slab phones, Samsung’s average revenue per unit will likely rise alongside increased volumes, directly improving profits. More profits will mean the company will invest more money into foldables to improve them further.  However, all of this newfound momentum will only be capitalized on if Samsung works fiercely to further improve its future foldables.  To stand toe-to-toe with the iPhone Duo, Samsung needs to push beyond its current IP48 ratings and finally make the Galaxy Z Fold 9 and the Galaxy Z Fold 9 Ultra IP68 certified. It must also bring S Pen compatibility to its future foldables and equip them with better front and rear cameras.  Samsung has single-handedly kept the foldable phone segment alive for years, and now, it is time to prove it can adapt and lead the market. Evaluating MSTR using conventional corporate finance metrics (such as Price-to-Earnings or EBITDA multiples) fails to capture the core driver of its equity valuation: the dynamic Net Asset Value (NAV) premium driven by programmatic Bitcoin treasury expansion. This technical article explores an end-to-end, reproducible quantitative pipeline built in R. Inspired by recent advancements in automated SEC parsing tools—specifically the secfile architecture highlighted in Interactive Brokers Quant Blog—this pipeline ingests real-time SEC EDGAR filings, dynamically extracts digital asset balance sheet facts, aligns mixed-frequency financial and market data, and models MSTR daily equity log returns using an out-of-sample 82.08% R-Squared structural tidymodels framework. Historically, extraction of balance sheet metrics directly from SEC filings (Forms 10-K and 10-Q) required brittle HTML regex scraping or costly third-party commercial APIs. Corporate disclosures often vary across reporting periods, particularly when handling emerging asset classes like digital currencies. MicroStrategy’s XBRL taxonomy has evolved, tagging Bitcoin holdings under varying terms such as DigitalAssets, CryptocurrencyHoldings, or within broader Assets line items. As demonstrated in the Interactive Brokers Quant Blog overview of secfile, direct ingestion of SEC EDGAR financial facts via compliant XBRL parsing solves three primary institutional hurdles: Using tidy evaluation via the rlang package, the pipeline dynamically isolates balance sheet events safely without breaking execution when SEC XBRL tags undergo structural revisions. The core hypothesis of this quantitative framework is that MSTR daily return dynamics are governed by two orthogonal components: Continuous log returns for asset prices are calculated by taking the natural logarithm of the current price divided by the previous day’s price. Taking natural logarithms guarantees additivity over time horizons and prevents non-negative boundary issues inherent to simple percentage returns. To quantify treasury expansion independently of market price fluctuation, the Balance Sheet Shock metric measures the logarithmic growth rate of total Bitcoins held on MicroStrategy’s balance sheet. Because corporate filings occur at discrete quarterly intervals, daily balance sheet values are carried forward using Last Observation Carried Forward via the zoo package. Consequently, the balance sheet shock value equals zero on non-reporting days, triggering discrete structural impulses only on filings or event reporting dates. The structural linear model specification expresses the daily log return of MSTR as a function of three main components: The pipeline follows a modern, production-grade functional programming architecture using the tidyverse ecosystem: Financial time series violate the Independent and Identically Distributed (i.i.d.) assumption of standard k-fold cross-validation due to autocorrelation. To preserve time order, we employ strict time-based windowing via timetk. Using recipes and workflows, we define the feature roles and couple them with a native Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) estimation engine. This guarantees clean execution without data leakage across the training split and testing horizon. Out-of-sample validation was conducted over a 15-day forward horizon, evaluating the structural model against a Naive Baseline Benchmark (1-day lagged return persistence model where predicted return equals yesterday’s actual return). The Structural Model achieved an out-of-sample R-Squared of 82.08%, significantly outperforming the Naive Baseline. This confirms that equity return variance in MSTR is predominantly explained by spot Bitcoin fluctuations and treasury balance sheet updates rather than simple price momentum. Log return forecasts are converted back into actionable nominal price predictions using exponential compounding anchored to the previous trading day’s close price. The predicted price equals yesterday’s closing price multiplied by the exponential of the predicted log return. Using the empirical Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) derived from out-of-sample evaluation, dynamic 2-sigma volatility boundaries are constructed around the predicted price path: By combining automated SEC EDGAR parsing via secfile package with functional machine learning pipelines in tidymodels, quantitative analysts can build scalable, production-ready asset pricing engines. In the case of MicroStrategy (MSTR), incorporating SEC XBRL balance sheet tracking alongside high-frequency spot crypto returns yields an empirical out-of-sample explanatory power (R-Squared) exceeding 82%.
